title: The Right Way to Balance Trade
gist: Wallach argues the WTO/FTA neoliberal trade order is being killed simultaneously by China's $1.2T surplus and Trump's incoherent tariffs, and proposes a successor: an open bloc of countries committing to collectively balanced trade, self-set tariffs under negotiated caps, strict rules of origin, ILO/environmental floors, and antimonopoly rules. Her key investable premise is that the U.S. trade deficit and its market-access leverage outlast Trump, and that the U.S. side of rebalancing must run through capital controls on foreign inflows rather than tariffs alone.

themes.theme: Neoliberal trade order as monopoly architecture

insights.claim: The WTO and modern free-trade agreements were a radical break from GATT because they forced signatories to conform domestic non-trade policy — services regulation, IP, procurement, food and product safety — to one-size-fits-all rules, rather than merely setting tariffs and quotas.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Frames trade renegotiation risk as regulatory-sovereignty risk: sectors that were protected by treaty-locked rules (pharma IP, digital services, procurement exclusion) are the ones exposed if the order is rewritten.
insights.quote: the WTO, NAFTA, and other agreements of the late twentieth and early twenty-first century were far more expansive, requiring signatory countries to conform their domestic policies to one-size-fits-all rules
insights.locator: THE PURPOSE OF A SYSTEM IS WHAT IT DOES

insights.claim: The WTO's TRIPS agreement mandates 20-year monopoly patents on medicines, and FTA intellectual property chapters layer on further protections that let pharmaceutical corporations charge higher prices — making global drug pricing a treaty artifact rather than a market outcome.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Pharma's international pricing power rests on a trade-treaty pillar an explicitly antimonopoly successor regime would target; watch IP chapters in any post-neoliberal negotiation as a pharma margin risk.
insights.quote: mandating that countries provide 20-year monopoly patents on medicines
insights.locator: They also required countries to adopt pro-monopoly policies

insights.claim: The WTO's General Agreement on Trade in Services bars signatories from regulating companies based on firm size or the number of services a single firm may offer, which functionally outlaws structural antitrust remedies in services.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
entities: General Agreement on Trade in Services
insights.so_what: Structural break-up risk for large financial and services conglomerates is currently suppressed by treaty; a regime change removes that shield.
insights.quote: forbids signatory countries from regulating companies based on firm size or the number of services any one firm is allowed to offer
insights.locator: They also required countries to adopt pro-monopoly policies

insights.claim: Digital trade chapters in the Trans-Pacific Partnership and USMCA undercut national ability to enforce Big Tech competition, data privacy and security, and AI oversight laws — making trade agreements the quiet defensive moat for large technology platforms.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: AI and platform regulation fights will be fought partly in trade text; erosion of digital trade chapters is a concrete regulatory-cost catalyst for large platforms.
insights.quote: pacts including the Trans-Pacific Partnership and the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement have added “digital trade” rules that undercut the ability of countries to enforce their own laws regulating Big Tech competition, data privacy and security, and AI oversight
insights.locator: Most recently, pacts including the Trans-Pacific

insights.claim: Investor-state tribunals embedded in most free-trade agreements can order governments to compensate investors when domestic policy changes conflict with investor expectations, which systematically penalizes raising wages or standards and rewards lowering them.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Explains why cross-border capital has been structurally biased toward low-standard jurisdictions; removal of ISDS raises the discount rate on politically exposed foreign direct investment.
insights.quote: countries are punished for seeking to raise wages or standards and rewarded for lowering their standards to attract foreign investment
insights.locator: By contrast, most free-trade agreements include

insights.claim: Lower consumer prices under the neoliberal order came not from efficiency but from labor abuses, lax environmental enforcement, currency manipulation, and multilayered subsidies the system failed to prohibit.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Implies the disinflation dividend of globalization was a transfer, not a productivity gain — so reversing it need not be as inflationary as consensus assumes, but the price floor rises where those practices are banned.
insights.quote: what really lowered consumer prices were labor abuses, lax environmental regulations that permitted the dumping of toxins into the air and water, and trade-distorting mercantilist tools the system failed to prohibit, including currency manipulation and massive multilayered subsidies
insights.locator: This global trade architecture was sold as more efficient

themes.theme: China's surplus mechanics and the U.S. deficit

insights.claim: China's trade surplus reached $1.2 trillion as of 2025, the largest in the world, built on currency devaluation, excess dollar reserve holdings, forced labor, wage suppression, repressed consumption, a weak safety net that forces high savings, and heavy production subsidies.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Anchors the scale of the imbalance any rebalancing scheme must absorb; the listed levers are the specific policy items to watch for signs of genuine Chinese adjustment.
insights.quote: As of 2025, China’s trade surplus stood at $1.2 trillion, the world’s largest.
insights.locator: DELAYED FUSE

insights.claim: The U.S. trade deficit peaked at $960 billion in 2022, and the accumulated deficit contributed to the shuttering of 70,000 American factories from the mid-1990s to 2023 plus at least five million manufacturing jobs lost between 2001 and 2020 per the Economic Policy Institute.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: The quantified political fuel behind bipartisan tariff support — the constituency for a post-neoliberal regime is measurable and does not disappear with an election.
insights.quote: This deficit contributed to the shuttering of 70,000 American factories from the mid-1990s to 2023 and the loss of at least five million manufacturing jobs between China’s admission to the WTO in 2001 and 2020
insights.locator: As critics at the time predicted

insights.claim: Dollars sent abroad for imports return as foreign purchases of high-yield speculative instruments, hedge funds, and buy-and-hold real estate rather than productive investment, so the trade deficit mechanically starves the real economy of financing while inflating asset prices and inequality.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: This is the core financial-channel argument: it implies U.S. asset valuations are partly a byproduct of the deficit, so any credible rebalancing is a headwind for speculative asset flows.
insights.quote: foreign firms and oligarchs, sovereign wealth funds, and state-owned enterprises seeking high returns channeled them into high-yield speculative financial instruments, hedge funds, buy-and-hold real estate speculation, and other nonproductive investments
insights.locator: Meanwhile, as the dollars spent by U.S. wholesalers

insights.claim: Both U.S. parties actively built the regime that enabled China's surplus — Clinton pushed the WTO through Congress in 1994 and greenlit China's accession in 2000, and Bush finalized it in 2001 while granting FTA or MFN status to a dozen countries including Vietnam and Singapore that China was already using as export platforms into the United States.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Transshipment through Southeast Asian platforms is presented as an original design flaw, not a new evasion — rules-of-origin tightening is therefore a durable, bipartisan policy direction to price into Vietnam/ASEAN export exposure.
insights.quote: Presidents in both parties championed the commerce regime that made China’s surplus possible.
insights.locator: U.S. presidents in both parties championed

insights.claim: COVID-19 supply shocks validated the warning shared by U.S. military planners and neoliberalism's critics that the United States had become dangerously reliant on other countries for essential goods.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: National-security framing is what converts reshoring from an economic preference into a defense-budget-adjacent mandate that survives political turnover.
insights.locator: The supply shocks of the COVID-19 pandemic

insights.claim: Fewer than 20 economies, mainly in Asia and Europe, run large chronic non-resource trade surpluses: over the past decade the Netherlands averaged 7.7 percent of GDP, Germany 7 percent, Switzerland 6.3 percent, South Korea 4.2 percent, Japan 3.6 percent, and Taiwan 13.4 percent.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: A named target list for any balanced-trade regime — these are the currencies and export sectors most exposed to a rebalancing mandate, with Taiwan the extreme outlier.
insights.quote: Taiwan’s has averaged 13.4 percent.
insights.locator: Today, world trade has become so imbalanced

insights.claim: Surpluses in Korea, Taiwan, and Germany are engineered through specific mechanisms — Korea repeatedly devalues the won, Taiwan subsidizes and intervenes in FX markets to cap Taiwan dollar appreciation, and Germany gains a currency advantage from the euro while suppressing wages via labor-law changes that expanded low-wage employment.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Names the exact intervention channels a rebalancing regime would force open — persistent FX undervaluation in TWD and KRW is the trade the framework implies unwinds.
insights.quote: Taiwan provides various subsidies and intervenes in currency markets to keep the Taiwan dollar from appreciating.
insights.locator: Governments have built these surpluses

insights.claim: Germany, holder of the world's second-largest chronic trade surplus, is now losing 10,000 industrial jobs per month because its firms cannot compete with subsidized Chinese goods redirected into Europe by U.S. tariffs.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Even surplus countries are now victims, which is the political precondition for Europe joining a bloc — and a live short thesis on European industrial incumbents facing Chinese import redirection.
insights.quote: Even Germany, which has the world’s second-largest chronic global trade surplus, is now losing 10,000 industrial jobs per month
insights.locator: In the European Union, a flood of Chinese imports

insights.claim: Large middle-income deficit countries are already acting unilaterally: Brazil, India, and Turkey have levied tariffs on Chinese steel, chemicals, furniture, plastics, electric vehicles, and industrial machinery.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Anti-China tariff walls are spreading beyond the West without U.S. coordination — Chinese export volumes face a broadening, not narrowing, set of barriers across emerging markets.
insights.quote: Brazil, India, and Turkey, for example, have levied tariffs on a number of Chinese imports, including steel, chemicals, furniture, plastics, electric vehicles, and industrial machinery.
insights.locator: On the other side of the ledger

insights.claim: The proposed successor regime requires balance across the bloc as a whole rather than bilateral balance between each pair of members, assessed on multiyear averages to allow year-to-year variation — a deliberate rejection of Trump-style bilateral deficit accounting.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a workable rebalancing architecture from the bilateral-deficit approach that has produced tariff chaos; multiyear group balance is the design detail to test any future policy proposal against.
insights.quote: Balanced trade would not mean that each participating country must have equal exports and imports with every other participant, but that overall trade within the group is balanced.
insights.locator: RULES OF ENGAGEMENT

insights.claim: Because the dollar is the reserve currency, the United States cannot rebalance through tariffs alone and would likely have to deploy capital-account tools such as capital controls on some foreign inflows to achieve and sustain balance.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: The single most market-relevant policy idea in the piece: capital controls on foreign inflows into U.S. assets would repriced Treasuries, real estate, and the dollar far more than any tariff schedule.
insights.quote: Washington would likely have to use tools on the capital account side of the ledger, such as capital controls on some foreign inflows, to achieve and sustain balance
insights.locator: If destabilizing surpluses were to arise

insights.claim: The bloc would differ from a customs union by letting each member set its own internal tariff rates below a collectively negotiated maximum trade-weighted internal rate and a binding top rate, preserving room for national industrial policy and tariff-rate quotas.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Signals the emerging policy consensus is flexible protection with caps, not free trade — plan for a permanently higher and more variable tariff baseline than the 1995-2016 era.
insights.quote: countries would be able to set their own tariff rates that apply to fellow participants, giving them the flexibility to enact industrial policies
insights.locator: BLOC PARTY

insights.claim: New entrants would have to unwind existing free-trade pacts with countries outside the bloc to prevent leakage, and members would enforce strict rules of origin — an explicit demand that joining means tearing up current agreements.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Sets an extremely high switching cost that makes the proposal slow to adopt; also flags transshipment-dependent economies as the structural losers of any such bloc.
insights.quote: as long as they unwound existing free-trade pacts with countries outside the bloc to avoid leakages, a tall order for some countries
insights.locator: To prevent goods from outside the bloc

insights.claim: Post-neoliberal arrangements would let members countervail against harmful subsidies quickly rather than through the WTO's lengthy timelines and methodological limits, so remedies arrive in time to save the affected industry.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Faster countervailing duties mean shorter lags between import surges and trade action — raises the volatility of tariff exposure for import-dependent supply chains.
insights.locator: As under the WTO, not all subsidies would be banned

insights.claim: If Chinese goods faced significantly higher tariffs across many countries simultaneously, Beijing might have no choice but to accommodate more domestic consumption to sustain its economy — making coordinated external tariffs the lever that forces Chinese rebalancing without China ever joining the bloc.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: The mechanism for the long-awaited Chinese consumption pivot is external coercion, not internal reform — watch coordinated multilateral tariff action as the leading indicator for Chinese consumer demand.
insights.quote: If Chinese goods faced significantly higher tariffs in many countries, Beijing might have no choice but to accommodate more domestic consumption to sustain its economy.
insights.locator: Although it is unlikely that Beijing would commit

insights.claim: Past trade pacts' labor and environmental enforcement failed because state-level fines let governments simply absorb violation costs as part of a low-road strategy to attract foreign investment.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Explains why existing labor chapters were never a real cost line — and why the next generation shifts penalties onto firms directly.
insights.quote: This effectively allowed those governments to absorb the cost of the violations as part of their “low-road” strategies to attract foreign investment.
insights.locator: When past trade pacts have included enforceable labor

insights.claim: The USMCA's Rapid Response Mechanism is the enforcement model to scale: individual firms — not governments — can face fines, tariffs, or loss of market access for violating labor rules, via a standardized review process and pre-agreed penalty guidelines.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Firm-level market-access penalties turn labor compliance into an idiosyncratic single-name risk rather than a diffuse country risk — a real diligence item for manufacturers with offshore plants.
insights.quote: individual firms can face fines, tariffs, or a loss of market access if they violate labor rules
insights.locator: Through the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement’s Rapid Response Mechanism

insights.claim: A multilateral antimonopoly framework already has a precedent: the never-implemented International Trade Organization proposed at Bretton Woods in 1945 included a Restrictive Business Practices chapter, which could be revived as enforceable bans on discriminatory pricing, cartelization, and corporate concentration.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Signals that competition policy is migrating into trade agreements — a channel through which multinational concentration could be attacked without any single national antitrust authority acting.
insights.quote: the International Trade Organization, the trade body originally proposed at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1945 but never implemented, included a Restrictive Business Practices chapter
insights.locator: Although the WTO has imposed anti-antitrust rules

insights.claim: Trump's tariffs have delivered neither the promised American manufacturing renaissance nor a coherent trade model other countries could adopt — a failure verdict delivered from the protectionist left rather than from free-trade defenders.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Critique from a trade-skeptic source means tariff policy lacks a durable constituency in its current form; expect redesign rather than repeal after the administration.
insights.quote: U.S. President Donald Trump’s chaotic and often misdirected tariffs have neither delivered the promised American manufacturing renaissance nor coalesced into an effective new model for trade other countries might adopt
insights.locator: Now, two forces are colliding

insights.claim: U.S. leverage over trading partners is structural rather than political: when Trump leaves office Washington will still hold the world's largest trade deficit, and as long as much of the world relies on selling into the U.S. market that leverage persists.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: The core investable premise: market-access coercion is a permanent feature of U.S. trade policy regardless of who wins, so exporters into the U.S. should assume conditionality is structural, not cyclical.
insights.quote: when Trump leaves office, Washington will still have the world’s largest trade deficit
insights.locator: AFTER THE CHAOS

insights.claim: The proposed rollout sequences the Americas and Africa first because trade there is already relatively balanced, then expands to Europe and Asia where chronic surpluses concentrate, with the UK as a likely early joiner and Germany, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan persuadable only by the threat of higher tariffs if they decline.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: A concrete geographic sequencing map: Latin America and Africa are the first-mover beneficiaries of any U.S.-led bloc, while surplus Asia faces coercive tariff pressure.
insights.quote: Large economies suffering from chronic trade deficits, such as the United Kingdom, would likely be keen to sign on
insights.locator: A new U.S. administration could use that leverage

insights.claim: The June 2026 G-7 summit issued a candid declaration affirming that extreme trade imbalances harm workers in surplus countries as well as deficit countries, indicating the surplus-country political consensus is already cracking.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: A dated, checkable marker that multilateral rhetoric has shifted toward imbalance-correction — the diplomatic precondition for coordinated tariff action against surplus economies.
insights.quote: as a surprisingly candid declaration from the June 2026 G-7 summit affirmed, extreme trade imbalances harm workers in deficit and surplus countries alike
insights.locator: Such a correction would benefit workers

insights.claim: Opposition to a new trade paradigm will come from two directions — oligarchs and monopolists defending the status quo, and politicians seeking to exploit Trump's tariff malpractice to restore the old free-trade order.
insights.speaker: Lori Wallach
insights.so_what: Frames the post-Trump policy fight as three-way rather than binary; a snap-back to pre-2016 trade rules is treated as a live but resisted scenario worth hedging.
insights.quote: from politicians hoping to exploit Trump’s tariff malpractice to revive the existing order
insights.locator: Growing bipartisan opposition to the old trade regime
